design_detail: Uncontrolled long-term follow-up of one cohort: the 19 people who received MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in the first US randomized phase 2 trial for chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD (Mithoefer et al., 2011; NCT00090064; 12 randomized to MDMA and 7 of the 8 placebo participants who crossed over to open-label MDMA afterwards), plus descriptive data on the one placebo participant who never received MDMA. The follow-up was added by protocol amendment after the trial had started; the first follow-up assessments took place 5 years after study initiation, and each participant was assessed once, 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session. Within-person comparison of the CAPS and IES-R scores obtained 2 months after the second MDMA session with the follow-up scores, plus an unvalidated questionnaire written by the investigators on benefits, harms, later treatment, drug use and perceived cognition. Sponsored and funded by MAPS. Read as the PMC author-deposited version of the SAGE article (CC BY).
can_establish: What the PTSD symptom scores, reported benefits and harms, later treatments and drug use of these 19 treated participants looked like, on average and one by one, a mean of about 4 years after their last MDMA session.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted psychotherapy caused the long-term outcome (there is no comparison group at follow-up, and most participants had later psychotherapy or psychiatric medicines), whether the average stability would hold in larger or less selected samples, or whether harm, dependence or cognitive decline were absent (a single yes/no question and self-reports from 19 people).

sample.recruitment: All 20 participants of the first randomized trial (Mithoefer et al., 2011) were mailed a consent form and a letter asking them to take part; all 20 took part (Methods and materials › Subjects, 3rd paragraph). The original trial enrolled people with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD, in most cases from sexual abuse or assault (Subjects, 1st paragraph); how they were recruited is not restated here.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in the original trial, which is not restated in this article. The Discussion gives a CAPS of 50 or more as the original entry criterion (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); the notes to Table 2 show that two MDMA-arm participants had CAPS 56 and 62 at enrolment and 43 after medication washout, the post-washout score being the one reported.
sample.demographics: The 19 MDMA-treated participants: 16 women and 3 men, mean age at enrolment 41.0; the 17 who completed the CAPS (including the participant who never received MDMA): 14 women and 3 men, mean age 42.3 (Subjects, 4th paragraph). Mean duration of PTSD symptoms more than 19 years (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph). Other demographics are in the original report.
sample.attrition: 3 of 19 MDMA-treated participants (16%) did not complete the CAPS and IES-R: one moved and was lost after answering the questionnaire; two declined, one of whom had shown the smallest CAPS reduction at 2 months and feared the testing would trigger symptoms, the other citing family stress (Subjects, 5th paragraph). All 20 completed the questionnaire.
sample.selection_effects: A small, highly selected group of treatment-resistant volunteers from a single private-practice trial. The crossover group consists of placebo participants who had not recovered with psychotherapy alone (the one who had recovered did not cross over and is excluded from the analysis). Follow-up intervals vary from 17 to 74 months because the follow-up was added late by amendment. Non-completers were compared with completers only on two questionnaire ratings, in groups of 16 and 3.

exposure.measurement: MDMA-assisted psychotherapy as delivered in the original trial: two 8-hour MDMA sessions 3 to 5 weeks apart with weekly non-drug psychotherapy, non-directive, following the sponsor's treatment manual; by a protocol amendment the last eight participants recruited (five in the double-blind and three in the crossover stage) had a third MDMA session, which came after the 2-month score used as this study's reference point (Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study design, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 notes).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses are not given in this article; the authors refer to the original report (Mithoefer et al., 2011), not read. Two or three sessions in all, by mouth.
exposure.polysubstance: At follow-up, by questionnaire under a certificate of confidentiality: cannabis by 8 participants (from 'once' to 'occasionally'), psilocybin mushrooms by 1 (frequency not reported), all of whom had used these substances before enrolment; one participant used 'ecstasy' once in a quasi-therapeutic setting. Participants had not been asked to abstain after the trial (Methods › Outcome measures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period). Psychiatric medicines: 12 of 19 at study entry and at follow-up (Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4). The authors call the MDMA pure; manufacture is not described here.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome was measured 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session.

comparison.controls: None at follow-up. The comparison is within person: CAPS and IES-R 2 months after the second MDMA session against the same participants' follow-up scores. The randomized comparison of the original trial ended before the crossover; the one participant who never received MDMA is reported separately (CAPS 14 at 2 months and 16 at follow-up; IES-R 5 and 15).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Intervening life events, reasons for continuing psychotherapy and treatments received outside those asked about were not measured; the authors suggest asking about life events in future questionnaires (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: CAPS (DSM-IV global severity and diagnostic status), given in person or by phone by the same independent rater who rated the original trial; IES-R, self-report by post; an unvalidated follow-up questionnaire written by the investigators (degree of benefit and persistence of benefit on 1 to 5 scales, a list of benefits, one yes/no question on harm, later psychotherapy and psychiatric medicines, use of 'ecstasy' and other illicit substances, perceived change in cognition, free comments). The NEO PI-R was given but is held back for a separate publication (Methods › Outcome measures; Study design, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: CAPS and IES-R are established instruments; the questionnaire is not validated, as the authors say (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Relapse is defined as a CAPS score above 50, the original entry cut-off.
outcomes.operationalization: Durability: no statistically significant difference between mean scores 2 months after the second MDMA session and at follow-up. Relapse: CAPS above 50. Harm: answering yes to whether one was harmed by taking part. Drug problems and cognitive decline: the participants' own answers to the questionnaire.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The six tests are CAPS and IES-R at 2 months against follow-up, two against three MDMA sessions for each, and completers against non-completers for degree and persistence of benefit; the rest is descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the rater knew that every participant analysed had received MDMA; the rater, Mark Wagner, is the second author and was paid by the sponsor to act as the independent rater (conflict-of-interest statement). All other outcomes are self-reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes reported. CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) at 2 months and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, matched t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), t 0.4, df 15, p = 0.72 (Table 1). Editors' calculation from the 16 completers' individual scores in Table 2, which reproduce the printed means and SDs: mean change −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, paired t), SD of the individual changes 31.4; 6 of 16 improved and 3 worsened by 10 points or more (by 14, 44 and 85 points). Mean pre-MDMA CAPS of the same 16 was 77.9 (for crossover participants the score after the placebo stage).
analysis.covariates: None. Two against three MDMA sessions were compared (CAPS t 0.2, df 14, p 0.83; IES-R t 0.7, df 14, p 0.48) and found not different, which was used to justify comparing everyone at 2 months after the second session (Study design, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The original trial is registered (NCT00090064, Acknowledgments). The follow-up was added by protocol amendment, approved by the Copernicus Group IRB, after the trial had started; no registration of the follow-up outcomes or analysis plan is mentioned (registry not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: NEO PI-R results withheld for a separate paper; the full questionnaire and all comments are online supplements on the sponsor's website (not read). The reference time point was chosen after a non-significant comparison of two against three sessions in 16 people.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 16 completers. The authors state that the sample is too small to compare participants who continued treatment with those who did not (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 of 19 treated participants, mean CAPS a mean of about 4 years after the last MDMA session was similar to the mean 2 months after the second session (23.7 against 24.6), with wide individual variation: two scores above 50 counted as relapses, and nine changes of 10 points or more in either direction. Three did not complete the CAPS. At follow-up 8 of 19 were in psychotherapy and 12 of 19 took psychiatric medicines. All 19 reported some benefit and none answered yes to having been harmed, on an unvalidated questionnaire; one reported using ecstasy once. There was no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title announces "absence of harmful effects or drug dependency", which rests on one yes/no question and self-reported drug use in 19 people, with no structured assessment of substance use disorder and no cognitive testing at follow-up. The Discussion reads the non-significant difference in 16 people as an enduring benefit of the treatment (the data are compatible with anything from a 17.6-point improvement to a 15.9-point worsening, editors' calculation) and argues that the improvement is not easily attributed to placebo or spontaneous remission, while the Limitations concede that there was no meaningful control group and that later psychotherapy and medicines confound the result. The Conclusions call the methodology rigorous and state that the results indicate a "favorable long-term risk/benefit ratio" (Conclusions, 1st paragraph).

timeline.event: Original randomized trial of 20 participants (Mithoefer et al., 2011, Journal of Psychopharmacology), the cohort followed here; not in the project's references.
This follow-up, 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session.

A pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials by an overlapping author group (Jerome et al., 2020, Psychopharmacology) appears; it was retracted on 10 August 2024 and is not evidence (METHODS §3.2).

Ponte et al. report 12-month open-label sleep and CAPS data pooled from four other phase 2 trials of the same sponsor; an expression of concern and a correction (4 participants removed) followed in December 2024.
The second phase 3 trial reports outcomes to 18 weeks only.

replication.where_it_stands: The only peer-reviewed long-term (more than 1 year) follow-up of a randomized MDMA trial that the project has found and that is not retracted. It describes one small cohort without a comparison group, and the same sponsor's later pooled follow-up was retracted. It can be cited for what was observed in these participants, not for an effect of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy at follow-up.

funding.funder: The Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), a non-profit organization (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The sponsor played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing of the report; the investigators collected the data. Three authors (Yazar-Klosinski, Jerome, Doblin) are employed by the sponsor. Michael Mithoefer is a medical monitor for other MDMA studies of the sponsor; he and Ann Mithoefer were paid by the sponsor for conducting this research and for work on a treatment manual, investigator training and protocols for further studies. The sponsor paid Mark Wagner for acting as the independent rater (Footnotes › Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The follow-up CAPS was administered by the second author, who was paid by the sponsor; the questionnaire was written by the investigators; the statistics author is a private biostatistics consultant (affiliation 7). The first two Mithoefers practise privately in Mount Pleasant, SC, and are affiliated with MAPS clinical research (author information).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial with long-term follow-up planned from the start, at fixed intervals, in which the comparison group is followed as long (or a randomized comparison with an established trauma-focused psychotherapy), with blinded raters, structured assessment of substance use disorders and cognition, and full recording of later treatments and life events.

domains.note: No comparison group at follow-up: whether scores stayed low because of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, later psychotherapy (8 of 19) or medicines (12 of 19), the natural course or life events cannot be separated, as the authors acknowledge.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Every MDMA-treated participant of the trial was approached and took part, but the crossover arm contains only placebo participants who had not recovered with therapy alone, and the treated cohort is a highly selected treatment-resistant group.
Who received two or three MDMA sessions is recorded for each participant (Table 2).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: After the reference point, 8 participants had a third MDMA session; during follow-up most had other treatment (psychotherapy, psychiatric medicines) and 8 used cannabis; none of this is accounted for in the analysis.

3 of 19 (16%) without CAPS, for reasons that may relate to the outcome (one feared symptoms would be triggered and had responded least); analyses are completers only, with a worst-case count given in text.

The CAPS rater knew all analysed participants had received MDMA, was paid by the sponsor and is a co-author; ratings by phone or in person; harms, drug use and cognition rest on an unvalidated self-report questionnaire written by the investigators.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Follow-up added by amendment with no reported analysis plan; NEO PI-R withheld; reference time point justified after the fact by a non-significant subgroup comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges a study's ability to estimate an intervention's effect. Without a comparison group at follow-up, and with co-interventions in most participants, this follow-up cannot estimate the long-term effect of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (critical confounding), and its outcome measurement is unblinded and partly unvalidated. It remains usable as a description of what was observed in these 19 people: mean CAPS similar to the 2-month score, wide individual variation, two relapses, and three participants without data. Claims may cite it in that descriptive sense only, never for an effect or for an absence of harm or dependence.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 20 people randomized in the original trial (12 MDMA, 8 placebo with the same psychotherapy); 7 of the 8 placebo participants accepted open-label MDMA afterwards, so 19 received MDMA; the eighth had recovered with psychotherapy alone. The last eight recruited had a third MDMA session (8 had three sessions, 11 had two).
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study design, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Follow-up added by protocol amendment; all 20 took part. 20 completed the questionnaire and 17 the CAPS and IES-R, of whom 16 had received MDMA (16 women and 3 men among the 19 MDMA-treated, mean age at enrolment 41.0). Three MDMA-treated participants did not complete the measures: one moved, two declined (one with the smallest earlier CAPS reduction feared the testing would trigger symptoms; one cited family stress).
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Timing: CAPS and IES-R 17 to 74 months after the final MDMA session (mean 45.4, SD 17.3, n = 17); questionnaire 10 to 74 months after completion (mean 40.8, SD 19.2, n = 20). The first follow-up assessments came 5 years after study initiation, so intervals vary widely.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 6th paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 16 MDMA-treated completers, CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) 2 months after the second MDMA session and 23.7 (SD 22.8) at follow-up, t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), t 0.4, df 15, p = 0.72.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Two of the 16 completers (13%) had CAPS above 50 at follow-up, which the authors call relapse to moderate-to-severe PTSD; counting the three non-completers as negative outcomes as well gives 5 of 19 (26%). The Discussion restates this as 14 of 19 (74%) with sustained reductions in the worst case and up to 17 of 19 (89%) at best.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the individual scores (Table 2), which reproduce Table 1's means and SDs: mean change from 2 months to follow-up −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9; paired t −0.11), SD of individual changes 31.4. Six of 16 improved by 10 points or more (largest 53 points) and three worsened by 10 points or more (by 14, 44 and 85 points; the two relapses went from 16 to 60 and from 6 to 91).
The participant who never received MDMA had a sustained response to psychotherapy with placebo: CAPS 14 at 2 months and 16 at follow-up; IES-R 5 and 15.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Questionnaire (19 MDMA-treated): all reported some benefit and all answered no to having been harmed by taking part. Degree of benefit: 11 (58%) rated it 5 ('large'), mean 4.3; persistence: 8 (42%) said benefits had lasted and continued to grow, 4 (21%) that some but not most had lasted, mean 3.8, median 4. Most endorsed benefits: general well-being and increased self-awareness 17 (89%) each, less excessive vigilance and less avoidance 15 (79%) each, fewer nightmares, flashbacks or intrusive memories 13 (68%), improved sleep 12 (63%).
key_findings.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Later treatment: at enrolment 16 of 19 (84%) were in psychotherapy, at follow-up 8 of 19 (42%), most often EMDR (4) and cognitive behavioural therapy (3). Psychiatric medicines: 12 of 19 at entry and at follow-up; mean number of medicines 1.7 at entry and 1.3 at follow-up. The authors call this the most important confounder of the durability finding.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participation in psychotherapy; Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4; Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text prints 58% for 12 of 19 (which is 63%); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Drug use during follow-up (self-report under a certificate of confidentiality): cannabis by 8 ('once' to 'occasionally'), psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom had used them before enrolment; one participant used 'ecstasy' once in a quasi-therapeutic setting and reported no interest in repeating it outside a legal therapeutic context. Participants had not been asked to abstain. No participant is reported to have developed a substance use problem; there was no structured assessment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period; Methods and materials › Outcome measures, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Risk of substance abuse

key_findings.finding: All participants answered yes to whether more MDMA sessions would have been helpful. On perceived cognition, none reported a decline; 7 reported no change and 13 an improvement (self-report only; no testing at follow-up).
key_findings.locator: Results › Opinion about additional sessions; Results › Cognitive function

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: no meaningful control group, because all but one participant ended up receiving MDMA, so natural history or uncontrolled variables could explain the results; follow-up intervals varied because the follow-up was added late; later psychotherapy and medicines preclude a definite conclusion about long-term benefit; blinding in the original trial had been transparent to the investigators and most participants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Symptom improvement and other benefits reported on our LTFU Questionnaire, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the 2-month and follow-up scores were compared with independent t tests and independent Mann-Whitney U tests, although they are the same participants; the abstract and Table 1 report a matched t with df 15.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods and materials › Study design, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the editors' paired calculation from Table 2 gives the printed t of about 0.1, so the reported result stands; the Methods text is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Psychiatric medicines: the text gives 58% (12/19) on medicines at entry and at follow-up, but 12 of 19 is 63%. In Table 4, participant 10's follow-up row shows an 'other' medicine (code f, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) but a follow-up total of 0, and the follow-up column total is 23 while the category totals add up to 24; the text's mean of 1.3 medicines corresponds to 24 of 19, and 12 participants are on a medicine at follow-up only if participant 10 is counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small: use the counts (12 of 19 at both times), not the percentage; the follow-up total in Table 4 is one short.

reporting_issues.issue: Perceived cognition: 7 participants with no change and 13 with improvement add up to 20, but the section reports on the 19 MDMA-treated participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two counts is wrong, or the non-MDMA participant is included; these self-reports should not be cited as counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Persistence of benefit: the text gives a median of 5 for the whole group, for the 16 CAPS completers and for the 3 non-completers, but Table 3 shows only 8 of 19 rating persistence 5 (median 4); a median of 5 among 16 completers would need at least 9 such ratings.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › LTFU questionnaire results › Degree of benefit, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The completer versus non-completer comparison of persistence (p = 0.18) cannot be reconciled with Table 3; cite Table 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the relapse rate as 'a minimum of 11% of the CAPS completers', but 2 of 16 completers is 13%, as the Results say; 11% is 2 of 19.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results › CAPS and IES-R, 2nd paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract presents the 17-to-74-month interval (mean 45.4, SD 17.3) as the follow-up of the 16 MDMA-treated completers, but the Methods give it for n = 17, including the participant who never received MDMA; from Table 2, the 16 completers' intervals average 45.6 months (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract; Methods and materials › Subjects, 6th paragraph; Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the claim; noted for accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: For the 8 participants who had a third MDMA session, the '2-month' reference score was taken before that session (Table 2 notes), so the comparison mixes scores after the full treatment with scores after part of it.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 2 notes; Methods and materials › Study design, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: For these participants the follow-up change includes the effect of the third session; the stability of the mean is partly built from different starting points.
